newsitem.title: USA: California extends cotton plowdown deadlines.
newsitem.headline: California extends cotton plowdown deadlines.

text.p: The California Department of Food and Agriculture said on Tuesday it had extended cotton plowdown deadlines for the San Joaquin Valley.
It said the deadline had been extended because recent flooding and foggy weather had made widespread harvesting activities there impossible.
"Recent adverse weather has created cases of extreme hardship throughout the San Joaquin Valley," California Agriculture Secretary Ann Veneman said.
"Agricultural commissioners and Cotton Pest Control Board members in the affected San Joaquin Valley counties agree that this extension is necessary," she added.
The San Joaquin Valley, which runs through the centre of the state, has been badly hit by floods.

The new plowdown deadline is January 31 for an area including Kern, Kings and Tulare counties and part of Fresno county. It is February 7 for an area including another part of Fresno county and all of Madera and Merced counties, the Department of Food and Agriculture said.

The plowdown deadline is designed to minimise over-wintering and break the life cycle of the pink bollworm. To comply with the plowdown deadline, cotton growers are required to shred all cotton plant debris and till the land on which cotton has been grown.
The pink bollworm, widely recognised as the most destructive of all cotton pests, burrows into the cotton boll, feeding on fibre and seed and irreparably damaging the crop.
If pink bollworm were established in the San Joaquin Valley, cotton growers' pest control costs would increase by $90 to $100 per acre, the department said.
Cotton lint ranks fifth among farm products in California with a value of more than $1 billion. California's crop accounts for more than 14 percent of U.S. cotton production, it added.
